og.og:description: Compare the real cost of receiving USD in Argentina. You can keep every dollar, there is no annual cap, and your bank may not charge you to receive it.

twitter.twitter:title: Receive USD in Argentina: real costs compared 2026
twitter.twitter:description: Compare the real cost of receiving USD in Argentina. You can keep every dollar, there is no annual cap, and your bank may not charge you to receive it.

@graph.headline: How to receive USD in Argentina: you can keep the dollars now

mainEntity.name: Do I have to sell the dollars I receive from abroad, or can I keep them?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can keep all of them, and this is the fact most sources get wrong. The central bank's rulebook requires service export receipts to be brought in within 20 business days, and then exempts a resident individual from the obligation to sell, provided the money is credited to a foreign currency account in your name at a local financial entity and the arrangement is fiscally neutral. There is no annual ceiling on that exemption. The USD 36,000 cap you will read everywhere was removed in September 2025, and in April 2026 the exemption was extended to all service categories, which means the lists of service concept codes you will find quoted for freelancers no longer limit which kinds of work qualify. The codes themselves have not gone away, and banks still use them to register these operations, so expect to be asked which one applies. Keep the distinction straight, though: the obligation to bring the money in survives. Only the obligation to convert is gone.

mainEntity.name: Does my bank charge me to receive a transfer from abroad?

acceptedAnswer.text: Your Argentine bank is not allowed to. The same provision that grants the dollar exemption says entities may not charge commissions on these operations, and then lets exactly one thing through: documented charges from the foreign intermediary banks in the transfer, passed on at cost. So there are two answers depending on what you mean. A commission quoted by your own bank on an inbound credit to a dollar account under these concepts is worth questioning with the rule in hand. Money missing because a correspondent bank took a cut on the way is not covered by the ban, and on a plain wire nobody has pre-funded it, which is why a wire can arrive short while Wise, which predicts those deductions on this corridor, does not. And you cannot stop your client's own bank charging them to send, which is what the figure in our table stands for.

mainEntity.name: Is the official rate still miles below the real one?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, and this is the other thing readers arrive with backwards. For years the spread between the official rate and the parallel market was so wide that it swamped every provider fee, and choosing how to convert mattered far more than choosing who to receive with. That is no longer the case. On 21 October 2026 Banco Nacion's board rate was 1,495 pesos to buy and 1,545 to sell, the MEP rate was within a peso or two of the official sell rate, and the informal rate was quoted anywhere from level with it to about 2% above it, depending on which aggregator you read. We should be clear about sourcing: the Banco Nacion board rates are primary, while the parallel and financial rates come from market aggregators rather than a regulator, and on the day we checked those aggregators did not agree with each other. The practical consequence is that a cheap provider now beats a clever rate, which has not been the case here for a long time.

mainEntity.name: Does Wise work for getting paid in Argentina?

acceptedAnswer.text: In two ways, and only one of them is a single step. Wise carries dollars to an Argentine bank account by SWIFT for a published Swift payout fee of $13.47, with the intermediary bank deductions predicted and pre-funded so you get the full amount. That is the figure in our table, with nothing added for the way your client pays in, because pushing a payment into your Wise details carries no percentage. Combined with the ban on your bank charging you to receive, that is the cheapest clean route here. Pesos are different. Your client cannot send pesos: Wise's US send page says it is not there yet and offers a waiting list. Wise does pay pesos out to any Argentine bank account, and you can reach that by converting dollars you already hold in your Wise account and sending them to your own CBU. You will need the full name, address, CBU and CUIT or CUIL, the pesos can only come from a conversion inside Wise rather than from an outside deposit, and Wise caps it at the equivalent of USD 18,000 per transfer, per calendar month. We have left that route out of our table rather than price it, because the only quotes we could get come from Wise's pricing system, which also returned dozens of priced dollars to pesos sends that its own send page says are not available.

mainEntity.name: How much can I invoice as a monotributista exporting services?

acceptedAnswer.text: The category ceilings run from about 12 million pesos at the bottom to roughly 126.6 million at the top, on the scale effective from August 2026, and export income counts toward them like any other income. At the late-October rate that top ceiling is around 83,000 dollars a year, which is the number a growing freelancer plans against. Those figures index periodically, so check the current table rather than our conversion. Above the ceiling you move to the general regime. One piece of good news: the tax authority says monotributistas do not have to register in the exporters' registry.

mainEntity.name: Do I charge IVA to a client abroad?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, though the reason differs depending on who you are. The VAT law places a service whose effective use or exploitation happens abroad outside national territory, and the same sentence gives it the treatment of article 43, which is the export regime: an exporter can set the VAT it was charged on related inputs against other tax it owes, and where that is not possible have it refunded or transfer it. So the accurate way to put it is that an export service is relieved of Argentine VAT and comes with a mechanism for recovering VAT you paid on the way, not that there is nothing to claim. Exports are separately exempt under article 8. If you are a monotributista the question falls away, because you are outside VAT regardless and have no input VAT to recover. Note too that the agency was renamed from AFIP to ARCA, and old AFIP addresses still serve live content, which makes it easy to mistake an old page for a current one or the reverse.

mainEntity.name: What do I keep as proof the money came from abroad?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no single certificate like the ones India or Bangladesh issue. What you keep is the export invoice, issued through the tax authority's system after enabling an export point of sale and carrying the destination country's tax identifier in the buyer field, together with the bank's settlement records for the operation. Where you invoice in pesos, the rate to use is the Banco Nacion buying rate from the day before you issue. Keep the invoice and the bank records together, because they need to tell the same story.

mainEntity.name: What if I get paid in USDT or USDC instead?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is common, and we are going to be straight about the limits of what we know. Nothing we read prohibits receiving stablecoins. The virtual asset providers now sit on a register run by the securities regulator, and registration is not the same thing as supervision of what they do. But nothing we read authorises a stablecoin receipt as a substitute for bringing the money in through the exchange market, and a payment that never touches that market does not produce the settlement record the dollar retention exemption is built on. So the route exists and is widely used, and whether it satisfies the obligation you are under is a question we cannot answer from the rules. That is a reading, not a ruling, and it is worth an accountant's time if you are relying on it.

mainEntity.name: Which tax form should I pick, and what is the rate for IT work?

acceptedAnswer.text: This is the decision worth the most money on the page. A sole trader can choose the progressive scale, a 19% flat tax, or the lump-sum ryczalt, and for software work the ryczalt rate is 12%. That figure is confirmed on the government business portal, which lists it against a specific set of statistical classification codes covering software-related services, software consultancy, software installation and network and systems management. Here is the nuance almost nobody states. Several of those entries carry the prefix meaning only part of the grouping is caught, so work that is genuinely not software-related is argued into the residual 8.5% service rate instead. On a 300,000 zloty year the gap between 12% and 8.5% is around 10,500 zloty. We have to be honest that the 8.5% route rests on individual tax interpretations and practitioner practice rather than a rule we read, and the boundary is settled case by case, so it is worth an accountant and possibly your own interpretation request. Two traps on the way there. First, the 5% regime for qualifying income from intellectual property is not a bonus you bolt onto the lump sum. It is charged on income, the tax portal sets it out alongside the scale and the flat tax, and the portal page that lists what a lump-sum taxpayer may actually claim does not mention it at all. So treat it as a reason to price the flat tax against the ryczalt rather than as a discount on the 12%, and have an accountant run both. Second, the step from 8.5% to 12.5% at 100,000 zloty is not the general rule for service income that English-language guides make of it, but it is not only about renting things either. The portal's list for that step includes research and development services, so a developer who classifies the work that way has chosen a bracket rather than a flat 8.5%. The rest of that list is accommodation, property rental and management, vehicle and equipment hire, and residential social care.

mainEntity.name: What will social contributions actually cost me?

acceptedAnswer.text: More than any transfer fee on this page, which is why we put it in the intro. On full contributions in 2026 the social package is 1,926.76 zloty a month, on a base of 5,652 zloty, and the government portal that publishes that total labels it as excluding the health contribution. Health is separate, and on the ryczalt it is a flat band by revenue: 498.35 zloty a month under 60,000 zloty, 830.58 from 60,000 to 300,000, and 1,495.04 above 300,000. Add the two and a developer on the ryczalt earning well is paying 3,421.80 a month, roughly 41,000 zloty a year, before any income tax at all. Two reliefs cut that at the start and both still exist, but neither one touches health, so read every relief figure as social only. Ulga na start gives six full months free of social, Labour Fund and Solidarity Fund contributions, and you still pay health in every one of those months, so your true floor is the health band rather than zero. Preferential contributions then run for 24 full months on a much lower base, 456.18 zloty a month in 2026, with health again on top, which puts the realistic bill in that period nearer 955 zloty. Both reliefs carry the same catch, and it is the one that bites Polish developers specifically: neither is available if you are providing the same kind of work to someone who employed you this year or last, which is exactly the employment-to-contract switch many people are making.

mainEntity.name: Do I charge Polish VAT to a US client?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The general business-to-business rule puts the place of supply where the customer has its business, so a service sold to a US company is supplied in the United States and is not taxed in Poland. The government portal works exactly that example and concludes the service is not subject to Polish VAT. Two refinements, both of which catch people. First, there is a genuine disagreement about what to write on the invoice: the government portal says to issue it without VAT marked as reverse charge, while Polish practitioners argue that reverse charge is the EU mechanism and does not apply to a US customer, and that the correct marking is the one meaning not subject to taxation, which is not the same as a 0% rate. We would rather report that conflict than pretend it is settled, so ask your accountant which marking they want. Second, if you are a registered VAT payer you do still report this income in your monthly VAT file, as a supply outside the territory of the country, even though no tax is charged. What does not apply is the EU sales listing, which covers EU customers only, so there is no summary information to file and no VIES check to run for a US client.

mainEntity.name: When do I have to register for VAT, and is it ever worth doing voluntarily?

acceptedAnswer.text: The exemption threshold for 2026 is 240,000 zloty, raised from 200,000 by an act of 24 June 2025 that took effect on 1 January 2026, and that same act carries a transitional rule letting a business with its seat in Poland whose 2025 sales exceeded 200,000 but stayed within 240,000 take the exemption this year. You need your business seat in Poland and must not be doing one of the excluded activities, which include legal services. Now the part most guides get backwards, and it matters a lot if all your clients are American. The threshold is measured on sales as the VAT Act itself defines that word, and the definition covers paid supplies of goods and services in the territory of Poland, the export of goods, and intra-EU supplies of goods. A service sold to a US business is supplied where the customer is, so it is none of those three, and the income from it does not push you toward the 240,000 limit. Polish tax commentary and published tax-office rulings read it the same way. We would still have an accountant confirm it against your own invoices before relying on it, because the cost of being wrong here is a backdated registration. On the voluntary question, there is a real argument for registering even though you owe nothing: the portal says you may deduct VAT on expenses related to providing the service where those expenses are taxed in Poland. That makes your laptop, your software and your office costs recoverable, which is why plenty of Polish freelancers with only American clients register anyway.

mainEntity.name: Do I have to use the national e-invoicing system for a US client?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, and this is the thing most likely to make an otherwise good guide wrong by omission. Structured e-invoicing through the national system became mandatory on 1 February 2026 for the very largest businesses and on 1 April 2026 for everyone else. A Polish freelancer invoicing a foreign business sits in no exclusion. There is a transitional easement until 31 December 2026, stated on the system's own official pages, letting you issue outside the system in a month where such invoices total no more than 10,000 zloty including VAT. The official wording is that they must not exceed 10,000, so 10,000 itself is still inside the easement, and once an invoice takes you past it you are in the system for the rest of that month with no way back. The practical question is what your client sees, and the system's own FAQ answers it directly: a foreign customer has no Polish tax identifier, cannot log in and cannot download the invoice, so you issue it in the system and then send the client the document separately however you have agreed, typically a PDF by email, carrying a QR code that lets them verify the invoice really exists in the system. So your workflow changes and your client's does not.

mainEntity.name: Can I invoice in dollars, and which exchange rate converts it?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can invoice in a foreign currency and in a foreign language: the rules do not prescribe the language, and a bilingual invoice is the common recommendation. On the rate, there are two separate rules and conflating them is a common mistake. For VAT purposes you use the National Bank of Poland average rate from the last business day before the tax point arises, or before the invoice date where the invoice comes first. For income tax you use the average rate from the last business day before the revenue arose. Both point at the bank's table A, and both mean the business day before, not the day itself. There is also an option to apply the income-tax conversion rule for VAT too, which then binds you for at least twelve months; we saw that referenced but did not open the page, so treat it as worth checking rather than settled.

mainEntity.name: Can I keep the dollars instead of converting them?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, and Poland makes this easier than any other country on this site because there is no currency law to satisfy. mBank's foreign-currency account is free to open and run and comes in ten currencies including dollars, so you can take a dollar payment, hold it, and sell when you choose. The catch is purely commercial rather than legal, and it runs the other way from most corridors here: Wise charges a published $27.24 to carry dollars to Poland by international transfer, against about $4.68 to convert and pay out zloty. So holding dollars costs noticeably more at ordinary invoice sizes. Do it because you want to choose when you sell, not to save money. And remember the spread is deferred, not escaped: you pay it whenever you convert, and if you let a Polish bank do the converting into a mismatched account it may cross twice.

mainEntity.name: What proof do I need that the money came from abroad?

acceptedAnswer.text: Less than readers arriving from other corridors expect, and it is worth saying plainly: Poland has no inward remittance certificate, no equivalent of the documents India or Bangladesh issue, and nothing to chase from your bank. What the government portal says to keep for a service treated as supplied outside Poland is documentation that the service was performed outside Poland and the EU, specifically a bank confirmation of payment and the contract with the client including any side arrangements. Add your e-invoice with its system number and QR code, and your revenue register if you are on the lump sum. That is the whole pack. On the American side, your client may ask you for a W-8BEN, which the US tax authority says a foreign person gives the payer whether or not they are claiming a reduced rate. Since personal service income is sourced where the services are performed, work done at a desk in Poland is foreign-source for US purposes and there is nothing for your client to withhold. The form documents that rather than claiming a treaty benefit, and we make no claim here about the treaty itself.

mainEntity.name: Do I have to sell my dollars, or can I keep them?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can keep them, and this is the most useful fact on the page because most readers arrive expecting the opposite. We read the National Bank's wartime resolution, the act that governs banking under martial law, in the consolidated text in force when we checked in October 2026, and there is no mandatory sale and no conversion obligation on a resident individual or a sole trader anywhere in it. The only forced sales in the document are aimed at banks rather than at you: a bank that bought currency for a client's medical treatment has to sell it back within two working days, and a bank holding currency on its National Bank account may sell it only to the National Bank. Neither touches a freelancer. The deeper reason is that Ukraine abolished mandatory sale of export proceeds in 2019, before the war, and the wartime rules did not reinstate it. We could not open the 2019 instrument itself, so treat that history as context rather than proof, but the current position does not depend on it: the resolution in force simply contains no such rule.

mainEntity.name: Is there a deadline for bringing the money into Ukraine?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is a 180 day settlement deadline in the resolution, and as written it covers goods rather than services. The point says the limit applies to operations involving the export and import of goods, and the word it uses is goods. Services are not named in it. We are not going to tell you that settles it, for two reasons we could not check. The currency law that sits above the resolution may define goods broadly enough to pull services in, which is how the older currency control regime worked, and we could not open that law's article text despite several attempts. And a separate 2019 resolution sets exceptions to those deadlines, which Ukrainian accounting press says removes service exports from bank supervision entirely, and that document refused us too. So the honest answer is that the deadline as written is about goods, and that you should not assume you are outside it. The Law on Foreign Economic Activity defines a good as any product, services, works, intellectual property rights and other non-property rights intended for sale, which is wide enough to reach a service export, and Ukrainian professional sources disagree among themselves about whether the settlement deadlines bite on services at all. The person to confirm it with is your own bank, because your bank is the one applying currency supervision to your account, and it is the one that will tell you whether your contract is in its file.

mainEntity.name: Which account should the money land in, my sole trader account or my personal one?

acceptedAnswer.text: Your sole trader foreign currency account, and this is not a preference. The National Bank's instruction on opening accounts requires a natural person to hold separate accounts for business or independent professional activity and for personal needs, and then says in terms that personal use accounts may not be used for operations connected with business activity. So client money in your personal account is prohibited by the account rules rather than merely untidy. The consequence when it happens is a tax one rather than a currency penalty. The tax service has advised more than once that money credited to a personal account, or left sitting inside a payment system, is not sole trader income at all: it is personal income, which is taxed at 18% plus the military levy instead of the 5% single tax. PrivatBank tells individual recipients the same thing on its own transfers page. We could not open the tax service's consultation ourselves, because its site refused us, so that number reaches you through Ukrainian accounting press rather than from the authority.

mainEntity.name: Can I move the dollars from my business account to my personal dollar card?

acceptedAnswer.text: Probably not directly, and we want to be straight that this is the weakest-sourced answer on the page. Ukrainian practitioners consistently cite a provision of the National Bank's currency regulation that forbids a sole trader transferring foreign currency from the business account to their own personal foreign currency account, with the described workaround being to sell the currency, move the hryvnia to your business hryvnia account, and transfer from there. We could not open that regulation at any address we tried, so we are reporting what practitioners say rather than a rule we read. Ask your bank before you plan around it. What we can tell you from a bank's own page is that monobank lets a sole trader move money to their personal account and withdraw up to 50,000 hryvnia a month without commission, which suggests the hryvnia leg of that workaround is routine.

mainEntity.name: Why will Wise not give me dollar account details?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because Ukraine is on the exclusion list, by name. Wise publishes an article on who can get dollar account details, and it lists the countries where having your address there disqualifies you; Ukraine appears on it, alongside Russia, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates and Serbia. Separately, Wise publishes the list of countries where you may hold money with it at all, and Ukraine is simply not there. So this is not a verification problem you can argue your way through, and it is not temporary as far as either page says. Wise does publish a dollar payout into PrivatBank accounts on domestic rails and a hryvnia payout to an IBAN, but not from the United States: for both it offers a waiting list rather than a transfer. So on a US corridor there is no Wise move for you and none for your client either. We should disclose that we earn a commission when someone signs up to Wise through this site, which is part of why we would rather spell this out than let you find it: on this corridor there is nothing for anyone to sign up to.

mainEntity.name: Does money sitting in Payoneer count as my income yet?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not as sole trader income, and the timing is where this gets expensive. The tax service's position, as reported by Ukrainian accounting press, is that funds sitting inside a payment system are not sole trader income: they become income when they reach your sole trader account. The trap is what happens if they never do. Money that ends up in your personal account instead is personal income at 18% plus the military levy rather than 5% plus 1%, and leaving a balance parked in Payoneer across a quarter end can leave you arguing about which period it belongs to. The practical habit is to withdraw to your sole trader foreign currency account and let the bank statement date the income. We could not open the tax authority's own page on this, so treat the rule as well attested rather than quoted, and ask your accountant how they date it.

mainEntity.name: What do I actually pay in tax on this?

acceptedAnswer.text: On the usual setup, a sole trader on the third group pays 5% single tax plus a 1% military levy, both on the hryvnia equivalent of what you received, converted at the National Bank's official rate for the date the money reached your account. The gross amount counts, before your bank's commission. The military levy on third group sole traders is the recent change that English language guides routinely miss: it arrived on 1 January 2025 and is charged on the same base as the single tax. Social contributions are separate. The levy's start date comes from the amending law itself on the parliament's site, but the rates in this answer reach you from Ukrainian accounting publications rather than from the tax authority, because the authority's site refused every request we made and the Tax Code page would not load either, so verify the current numbers before you rely on them. One thing worth noticing: this is the real cost of the corridor. Tax on a five thousand dollar month runs to roughly 300 dollars, while the entire argument about which provider to use is worth perhaps 40.

mainEntity.name: Does the 2% wartime single tax rate still exist?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, as far as we can establish, and this is the single most common stale belief about Ukrainian freelance tax. The 2% rate was a wartime measure and it was abolished from 1 August 2023. We are flagging it rather than stating it flatly because the law that repealed it refused to load for us, so we have this from accounting press rather than from the statute. If you are reading a guide that still quotes 2%, check its date before anything else: it is the fastest way to tell whether the rest of the page is current.

mainEntity.name: Can I use Diia City and its 5% rate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Almost certainly not, and the reason is who the regime is written for. The 5% personal income tax attaches to salary and to gig contract pay handed out BY a company that is a Diia City resident, and that resident is a Ukrainian legal entity which has to keep meeting monthly tests, reported as an average remuneration floor and a minimum headcount of employees and gig specialists. A sole trader invoicing a US client directly is nobody's gig specialist, so the regime does not reach you. It becomes relevant if you stop freelancing and join a Ukrainian company inside the regime. Our sources here are a professional services brochure and Ukrainian tax press, because the Diia City site did not resolve for us and the law itself would not load, so treat the thresholds as indicative.

mainEntity.name: Does my bank charge me to receive the transfer?

acceptedAnswer.text: On the two banks whose tariffs we could open, no. monobank states that receiving an incoming transfer is free. PrivatBank charges nothing on a personal current account or a premium card, and 1% on its payout and internet cards, while noting that correspondent banks in the chain may take their own cut depending on whether your client chose to pay those charges. PrivatBank's package for IT sole traders prices opening and monthly servicing at nothing, and its IT business page credits incoming payments up to a 17:00 cutoff rather than at any hour. What you cannot avoid is your client's own bank charging them to send, which is the figure in our table. One gap worth naming: neither bank publishes an inbound commission for a sole trader foreign currency account specifically, so the free figure is read off personal account and package schedules rather than a sole trader tariff.

mainEntity.name: What paperwork proves the money came from abroad?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no certificate here, and readers arriving from other corridors are often surprised by that. Ukraine issues no equivalent of the inward remittance certificates India or Bangladesh provide, and there is nothing to chase from your bank afterwards. What you keep instead is the statement on your sole trader foreign currency account showing the credit and its date, the contract or the invoice where the invoice works as a public offer, an act of services where your client signs one, and whatever your bank put in its own currency supervision file. Foreign language documents generally need a Ukrainian translation. The closest thing to a form we found is a bank's own process rather than a regulator's: PrivatBank runs a simplified currency control process for IT sole traders, says payments up to the equivalent of 400,000 hryvnia are credited automatically, and gives freelancers paid under platform offers from Upwork, Google and Payoneer an automated way to send foreign trade documents to the bank. We could not confirm the letter on the bank's own template that some guides describe, so ask the bank what it wants before your first credit.

mainEntity.name: Do I need to worry about the US side, or a tax treaty?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is a treaty, and the guides telling you otherwise are wrong, which is worth knowing because several of the pages ranking for this question say Ukraine has no tax treaty with the United States. It does: an income tax treaty signed in 1994 which entered into force in 2000. In practice your US client will ask you for a W-8BEN. Income from services is sourced where the services are performed, so work done at a desk in Ukraine is foreign source for US purposes and there is nothing for your client to withhold. The form documents that rather than claiming a treaty benefit. We make no claim here about what the treaty itself gives you on any particular kind of income, because that depends on the article and on your circumstances.

acceptedAnswer.text: Payoneer does not publish one, and that is a real answer rather than a dodge. It publishes 1% to receive a commercial payment and a withdrawal conversion cost given as a range of 1.2% to 4%, with no public rate feed behind it. So the only exact rate is the one shown in your account at the moment you withdraw. What you can plan with is the gap: start from today's mid-market rate above, then expect to lose roughly 2.2% to 5% of the payment across the two Payoneer charges together, and possibly more on a small payment, because the Payoneer fee schedule says that in some countries a minimum fee of up to 20.00 USD or equivalent may apply, and it does not say which. Our table models the midpoint of the published band because a range is not a price, and we flag it as an estimate for that reason.

mainEntity.name: Why is the Payoneer exchange rate lower than the rate on Google?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because the rate on Google is the mid-market rate, which has no margin in it and is not offered to retail customers by anyone. Payoneer takes its conversion cost inside the rate it gives you rather than showing it as a separate line, which is why the two numbers never match and why the difference is easy to miss. That is also why we price everything on this site as a distance from the mid rather than quoting rates: a rate quoted without the mid next to it tells you nothing about what it costs.

mainEntity.name: What exchange rate does Payoneer use?

acceptedAnswer.text: Its own. Payoneer converts at a rate it sets, which sits some distance below the mid-market rate, and it describes that distance only as a band of 1.2% to 4% for a withdrawal that involves conversion. It does not say where Pakistani rupees fall inside the band, and it does not publish the rate itself anywhere outside your account. The closest you can get to checking it is what this page does: take the mid-market rate at the moment you withdraw, compare it with the rate on your withdrawal screen, and the difference is what the conversion cost you.

mainEntity.name: Is Payoneer the cheapest way to get USD into a Pakistani bank account?

acceptedAnswer.text: For a client payment, yes, at every amount on this page. Payoneer is the cheapest of the routes we rank for Pakistan. Our Pakistan page does show one lower price, from Western Union, but lists it without ranking it: that number is Pakistan Remittance Initiative pricing, a home remittance scheme, and both Western Union's terms and the scheme itself describe it as being for personal transfers rather than client payments. Western Union publishes no commercial rate for this corridor. Its 1% receive fee is reasonable and the undisclosed withdrawal conversion is what costs you. What keeps most Pakistani freelancers on it anyway is that Upwork, Fiverr and many direct US clients pay into it with no effort from the client, and a cheaper route you cannot persuade a client to use is not cheaper in practice.

mainEntity.name: Does the 1% receiving fee apply to Upwork and Fiverr payments?

acceptedAnswer.text: Payoneer's charge of 1% is on incoming commercial payments, which is what a marketplace payout is. The thing to watch is that the marketplace usually takes its own cut first, so the 1% applies to what reaches Payoneer rather than to what your client was invoiced, and the two can be a long way apart. Check what your Upwork or Fiverr statement says left the platform, not what the client paid, and apply the figures below to that.

mainEntity.name: Which Pakistani banks does a Payoneer withdrawal reach?

acceptedAnswer.text: Our Pakistan page records HBL, UBL, MCB and Meezan as working reliably, with HBL and Meezan having official real-time withdrawal integrations with Payoneer. There is also an announced Payoneer route to a JazzCash mobile wallet, marketed as near real time rather than the one to three days a bank withdrawal usually takes. Neither company publishes a clear fee for the wallet route and third-party guides disagree about what it costs, so check the fee and the rate quoted in your own account before using it. If you claim the 0.25% PSEB tax rate, confirm with your bank or tax adviser that a wallet withdrawal still gives you the documentation you need.

mainEntity.name: What is the Payoneer to JazzCash dollar rate today?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no separate published rate for it. The JazzCash route is a Payoneer withdrawal to a mobile wallet instead of a bank, so the dollars are converted by Payoneer at its own rate, the same way as any rupee withdrawal, and neither company publishes a clear fee or rate for the wallet route. Third-party guides quote figures that disagree with each other. Before you use it, compare the rupee amount your Payoneer withdrawal screen shows for JazzCash with the amount it shows for your bank at the same moment. If the wallet amount is lower, the difference is the price of speed. Do not confuse this with the Request a Payment option in the JazzCash app. That sends your client a Payoneer payment link, and the money lands in your Payoneer account, not the wallet, so you still withdraw it afterwards.

mainEntity.name: How often does this page update?

acceptedAnswer.text: The mid-market rate on it refreshes hourly from our rate source, and the date and time of the rate publication are printed next to it so you can see how fresh it is rather than trusting us. The Payoneer fee figures change far less often and are re-checked on a weekly rotation against Payoneer's own published pricing, with the last check date shown at the foot of the page. If you spot a figure that no longer matches Payoneer's own page, that is worth more to us than a compliment.

mainEntity.name: Why is the Payoneer dollar rate lower than the bank rate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually because it is further from the mid-market rate. Bangladeshi banks convert an incoming wire at their TT buying rate, which banks do not usually publish as a distance from the mid (our Bangladesh table assumes about 1.5% below it), and Payoneer's conversion cost is given as 1.2% to 4%. But a bank rate is not the whole cost of a wire. Your client's US bank usually charges $25 to $45 to send it and an intermediary bank can take a cut, so on a $500 payment the wire can still lose more in total. On payments of a few thousand dollars the bank route often wins. Our Bangladesh page compares the two at different amounts.

mainEntity.name: Is Payoneer to bKash cheaper than Payoneer to a bank account?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually not. The 1% receiving fee applies either way. After it, Payoneer charges roughly 3% plus $1 per transfer to convert for the bKash route as of mid 2026, against 1.2% to 4% for a bank withdrawal. Then bKash charges to cash out: 18.50 Taka per 1,000 at a standard agent, or 7 Taka per 1,000 if you cash out Payoneer money at a BRAC Bank, City Bank or participating Q-Cash ATM. On a $1,000 payment the bank route comes out about a percentage point ahead at the middle of Payoneer's range (about 3.6% against about 4.7% with the ATM cash-out), and the two only draw level if your Payoneer conversion lands at about 3.8%, near the top of the range. The bKash route is faster, usually a few hours instead of one to three business days. Check both fees in the Payoneer portal and the bKash app before you rely on these figures.

mainEntity.name: Does a Payoneer withdrawal count for the 2.5% freelancer incentive?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only a withdrawal to a bank account can, because the incentive needs a Foreign Inward Remittance Certificate and only a bank issues one. Payoneer to bKash produces no certificate, and bKash's own Payoneer page says the government incentive does not apply to that service. Bangladesh Bank confirmed the 2.5% rate for individual freelancers for the year from 1 July 2026, and these incentives are expected to be phased out around the country's graduation from least developed country status, so check the current position with your bank before counting on it.

mainEntity.name: How much can I send from Payoneer to bKash at once?

acceptedAnswer.text: bKash is reported to set a minimum of 1,000 Taka and a maximum of 250,000 Taka per transfer, which is a little over $2,000 at mid 2026 rates. A larger payout has to be split across several transfers or sent to a bank account instead. Check what the Payoneer withdrawal screen will accept before you plan around the bKash route, and make sure your bKash account is fully verified against the same name Payoneer holds for you, since a name mismatch is a common reason a first transfer fails.

The Payoneer fees change far less often and come from the same data as our Bangladesh page, which is re-checked against Payoneer's published pricing on a weekly rotation.
